title: Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a Hangover: Which Works Better?
excerpt: Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover, compared honestly: electrolytes, sugar, and cost per serving, what rehydration actually fixes, and when plain water is enough.
metaDescription: Pedialyte vs Gatorade for a hangover: sodium, potassium, sugar, and cost compared, what rehydration actually fixes, and when plain water is enough.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** on paper, Pedialyte beats Gatorade for hangover rehydration. It has roughly twice the sodium, several times the potassium, and less than half the sugar per serving, because it was designed as a medical rehydration product rather than a sports drink. But here's the part most articles skip: rehydration only treats *part* of a hangover. Dehydration causes the dry mouth, the thirst, and some of the headache. It does not cause the nausea, the fatigue, the brain fog, or the general feeling of having been poisoned. Those come mostly from how your body processes alcohol itself. So either drink can help you feel somewhat better, neither one fixes the morning, and for a mild hangover plain water and a salty breakfast do most of the same job for free. This guide walks through the real numbers, when the difference actually matters, and what to do if you want to go after the cause instead of the symptoms.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares consumer products and summarizes general research in plain language. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** you can't keep fluids down for more than a day, you have signs of severe dehydration (dizziness when standing, confusion, very dark urine, little or no urination), you have kidney disease, heart failure, or high blood pressure and need to watch sodium, or your "hangovers" are getting worse or happening after small amounts of alcohol. If someone can't be woken after drinking, call 911 — that's possible alcohol poisoning, and no drink fixes it.

## Pedialyte vs Gatorade: The Numbers Side by Side

The two products were built for different jobs, and the labels show it. Pedialyte is an oral rehydration solution: a medical-style formula originally made for children losing fluids to vomiting and diarrhea. Gatorade is a sports drink: built for athletes who are sweating for hours and want something that tastes good enough to keep drinking.

Here's how they compare per 12-ounce serving, using the standard versions of each (Pedialyte Classic and Gatorade Thirst Quencher). Exact numbers vary a little by flavor and format, so check your label, but the pattern holds across the lineup:

| Per 12 fl oz | Pedialyte Classic | Gatorade Thirst Quencher |
|---|---|---|
| Sodium | ~370 mg | ~160 mg |
| Potassium | ~280 mg | ~50 mg |
| Sugar | ~9 g | ~21 g |
| Calories | ~35 | ~80 |
| Typical cost per serving | ~$1.50–2.00 (bottle), ~$1.00–1.50 (powder packs) | ~$0.60–1.00 |
| Where to buy | Pharmacies, grocery stores | Everywhere |

Read that table and the design difference jumps out:

- **Pedialyte has roughly 2 times the sodium and 5 times the potassium.** Sodium is the electrolyte that matters most for pulling water back into your system and holding it there. Potassium matters too, though you lose less of it.
- **Gatorade has more than twice the sugar.** That's deliberate. Sugar is fuel for athletes mid-workout and it makes the drink taste good. For someone lying on a couch with a queasy stomach, it's just extra sugar, and a big sugary drink can make nausea worse for some people.
- **Gatorade is cheaper and easier to find.** A bottle costs a dollar or two at any gas station. Pedialyte usually means a pharmacy aisle and more money, though the powder sticks bring the per-serving price down.

One more player worth knowing about: **Gatorlyte**, Gatorade's own rapid-rehydration line. It exists because Gatorade knows the classic formula is light on electrolytes for serious fluid loss. Gatorlyte carries a much higher electrolyte load and less sugar than regular Gatorade, which puts it close to Pedialyte territory. If the store only has Gatorade products, it's the closer match.

## Why Pedialyte Is Built the Way It Is

Pedialyte's formula comes from one of the quiet success stories of modern medicine: oral rehydration therapy. Researchers studying diarrheal disease found that your small intestine absorbs water fastest when sodium and glucose arrive together in the right ratio, because they share a transport system in the gut wall. Give someone the right mix of salt, a modest amount of sugar, and water, and you can rehydrate them nearly as well as an IV drip in many cases. The World Health Organization built its standard rehydration salts on this principle, and it has saved millions of lives.

Pedialyte is a consumer version of that idea: enough sodium to drive absorption and replace what you've lost, just enough sugar to power the transport system, and not much more. That's why it works for sick kids, food poisoning, stomach bugs — and why it became a hangover staple without the company ever needing to market it that way.

Gatorade came from a different problem. It was developed in the 1960s for University of Florida football players sweating heavily in brutal heat. Athletes lose a lot of water and some sodium through sweat, but they also burn carbohydrate, so the formula leans toward sugar for energy and flavor, with a lighter touch of electrolytes. That's a reasonable design for a long workout. It just isn't a rehydration formula in the medical sense.

So when people say "Pedialyte is Gatorade for adults who feel terrible," they have it backwards. Pedialyte is the medical product; Gatorade is the sports product that people reach for because it's in every cooler in America.

## The Honest Part: Dehydration Is Only One Piece of a Hangover

Here's where this article parts ways with most of the internet. The common story is: alcohol dehydrates you, dehydration causes the hangover, so rehydration cures it. The first part is true. The rest is only partly true.

Alcohol does dehydrate you. It suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate out more fluid than you take in. That's why you break the seal at the bar and wake up with a desert mouth. Dehydration contributes real symptoms: thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness, and some of the headache.

But researchers who study hangovers directly — there's a scientific group dedicated to it, the Alcohol Hangover Research Group — have consistently found that dehydration doesn't explain most of the misery. A few inconvenient facts:

- **Rehydrating doesn't make a hangover go away.** Studies where people drank water alongside or after alcohol found it improved thirst and dry mouth but did little for overall hangover severity. If dehydration were the whole story, water would be the cure. It isn't.
- **Hangover severity doesn't track hydration status very well.** You can be fully rehydrated and still feel awful, because the other mechanisms are still running.
- **The bigger culprits are the alcohol itself and its breakdown products.** When your liver processes alcohol, it first converts it to **acetaldehyde**, a toxic compound considerably nastier than alcohol, before breaking that down further. Alcohol and acetaldehyde also trigger an inflammatory response — the same messenger chemicals your immune system releases when you're sick, which is why a bad hangover feels like the flu. Add in disrupted sleep (alcohol wrecks the second half of the night), stomach irritation, low blood sugar, and congeners (byproducts in darker drinks like bourbon and red wine), and you have the real recipe.

What this means practically: **Pedialyte and Gatorade treat the dehydration slice of your hangover — the thirst, the dry mouth, some of the headache and lightheadedness. They do not touch the acetaldehyde, the inflammation, or the wrecked sleep.** Anyone who tells you an electrolyte drink "cures" a hangover is selling something. You'll likely feel somewhat better after rehydrating. You will not feel fine.

## When Pedialyte's Extra Sodium Actually Matters

Most mornings, the gap between the two drinks matters less than the marketing suggests. But there are situations where Pedialyte's medical-grade formula earns its price:

- **You threw up.** Vomiting dumps fluid and electrolytes fast, and it's the scenario Pedialyte was literally designed for. This is the clearest case for choosing it.
- **It was a long, heavy night.** More alcohol means more fluid loss over more hours, often with little food. Bigger deficit, more reason for the higher-sodium formula.
- **You were sweating too.** A summer wedding, a night of dancing, a festival. Alcohol plus sweat is a double drain, and sweat takes sodium with it.
- **You can't face food.** A salty breakfast is a perfectly good electrolyte delivery system, but only if you can eat it. If your stomach says no, a low-sugar rehydration drink gets salt in without asking your gut to digest much. Pedialyte's lower sugar is also gentler if you're queasy.

And when is plain water enough? More often than you'd think:

- **You had a few drinks and ate dinner.** Food comes with plenty of sodium. Water plus a normal breakfast covers you, and you can keep your five dollars.
- **Your symptoms are mild.** Thirst and a dull head respond to water, food, and time. The electrolyte drink mostly buys you convenience and placebo.
- **You just prefer it.** There's no evidence that healthy adults with mild hangovers need commercial electrolytes. Humans rehydrated with water and food for all of history.

One honest warning in the other direction: don't chug plain water by the liter on a badly depleted stomach while eating nothing. Water without any salt replaces fluid but not electrolytes, and extreme versions of that (many liters, fast) can dilute your blood sodium. That's rare and takes real effort, but it's the one scenario where "just drink more water" is bad advice. If you've lost a lot of fluid, pair water with salt from food or a rehydration drink.

## The Verdict

**For rehydration quality: Pedialyte wins.** More sodium, more potassium, less sugar, built on actual rehydration science. If you're genuinely depleted — vomiting, heavy night, sweating — it's the better tool, with Gatorlyte as a respectable second when it's all the store has.

**For mild mornings and convenience: Gatorade is fine.** It's cheap, it's everywhere, it tastes like your childhood, and for a run-of-the-mill hangover the difference between "some electrolytes" and "optimal electrolytes" is small. Half water, half Gatorade even fixes some of the sugar problem.

**For value: water plus salty food beats both.** Eggs, toast, a banana, maybe some pickle juice if you're feeling bold. Same electrolytes, more nutrients, zero dollars extra.

**For actually fixing the hangover: none of the above.** Rehydration improves the symptoms that come from fluid loss and nothing else. The rest of the hangover rides on how much you drank and how your body processed it — which was decided last night, not this morning.

If you want a deeper ranked list of morning-after options, including medical-grade oral rehydration salts and lower-sugar alternatives, our [best hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) guide covers the whole field honestly.

## The Better Play: Work on the Cause, Not Just the Morning

Everything above is symptom management. If you keep finding yourself googling electrolyte drinks at 9 a.m., the higher-leverage moves all happen *before and during* drinking, not after:

- **Drink less, and slower.** Unsatisfying but true. Hangover severity tracks total alcohol more than any other factor. Our [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) guide covers the habits with the best evidence — pacing, food, lighter-colored drinks, water between rounds.
- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption, which lowers the peak your liver has to deal with.
- **Consider DHM before you drink.** Dihydromyricetin (DHM) is a plant extract from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for how it affects alcohol metabolism — including the acetaldehyde step that rehydration can't touch. The honest status of the evidence: encouraging animal and lab data, limited human trials, promising but not proven. It is not a license to drink more, and it won't rescue a night of genuine excess. But unlike an electrolyte drink, it's at least aimed at the cause. If you want to try it, the two picks we rate highest are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines 1,000 mg of DHM with L-cysteine and electrolytes (covering the hydration angle too), and the budget option [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), pure 1,000 mg DHM at under a dollar a serving. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, the [dosage calculator](/dhm-dosage-calculator) personalizes it, and our [full reviews](/reviews) compare every major brand.

A sensible stack for a big night, if you want one: eat a real dinner, take DHM before drinking, alternate alcohol with water, and keep a Pedialyte or some powder packs on the nightstand for the morning. Each piece handles a different part of the problem. None of them makes heavy drinking consequence-free.

## The Bottom Line

- **Pedialyte beats Gatorade for rehydration**: about twice the sodium, several times the potassium, half the sugar. It's a medical product; Gatorade is a sports drink.
- **The difference matters most when you're truly depleted** — vomiting, a heavy night, sweating. For a mild hangover, either works, and water plus salty food works too.
- **Neither one cures a hangover**, because dehydration is only part of the problem. Acetaldehyde, inflammation, and bad sleep cause most of the misery, and no electrolyte drink reaches them.
- **Gatorlyte is Gatorade's closer answer to Pedialyte** if the store runs out of options.
- **The real wins happen before you drink**: less alcohol, more food, water between rounds, and optionally DHM aimed at the metabolism side.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Pedialyte or Gatorade better for a hangover?**

Pedialyte, on the numbers. Per 12 ounces it has roughly 370 mg of sodium and 280 mg of potassium with about 9 g of sugar, versus roughly 160 mg sodium, 50 mg potassium, and 21 g of sugar in regular Gatorade. More of the electrolytes that drive rehydration, less than half the sugar. That said, for a mild hangover either one helps with the dehydration part, and neither fixes the rest of the hangover.

**Does Pedialyte cure a hangover?**

No. It treats dehydration, which causes the thirst, dry mouth, and some of the headache. Most hangover misery — nausea, fatigue, brain fog, the flu-like feeling — comes from alcohol's breakdown products like acetaldehyde, inflammation, and disrupted sleep, and rehydration doesn't touch those. Expect to feel somewhat better after Pedialyte, not fine.

**Can I just drink water instead of Pedialyte or Gatorade?**

Usually, yes. If you had a moderate night and you're eating normally, water plus a salty breakfast replaces fluid and electrolytes without costing extra. The commercial drinks earn their keep when you're badly depleted — vomiting, a very heavy night, lots of sweating — or when you can't face food and need salt in liquid form. Just don't chug liters of plain water on an empty stomach while badly depleted; pair water with some salt from food or a drink.

**Should I drink Pedialyte before bed after drinking?**

It's reasonable and may make the morning somewhat gentler, since you're replacing fluid before the deficit peaks overnight. Keep expectations modest: pre-bed fluids improve the dehydration symptoms, not the hangover itself. A glass of water with a snack does most of the same job. If you're nauseous, sip slowly rather than chugging.

**Why does Pedialyte have more electrolytes than Gatorade?**

They were designed for different jobs. Pedialyte is an oral rehydration solution built on the medical science of sodium-glucose transport in the gut — high sodium, modest sugar — originally for children losing fluids to illness. Gatorade was built for athletes mid-exercise, who want carbohydrate for fuel and a taste they'll keep drinking, so it's higher in sugar and lighter on electrolytes.

**What about Gatorade Zero or Gatorlyte?**

Gatorade Zero drops the sugar but keeps the same modest electrolyte levels, so it's hydration-neutral — fine, not special. Gatorlyte is the one to grab: it's Gatorade's rapid-rehydration line with a much higher electrolyte load and less sugar than the classic drink, putting it close to Pedialyte. If the gas station has Gatorlyte, the Pedialyte advantage mostly disappears.

**Does anything actually prevent a hangover?**

Only drinking less, drinking slower, and eating properly have strong evidence. Beyond that, DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant extract studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, including the acetaldehyde step — the research is promising but still limited in humans, so treat it as a possible edge, not a shield. Electrolyte drinks, for their part, treat morning symptoms rather than preventing anything. See our [prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) for the full evidence rundown.
